doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Difficult studio moments on film soundstages
summary: He tells of isolation booths, lost cues at Warner Brothers and old Paramount film sessions.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well just a couple more things before we wrap up. I wondered, do you recall the most difficult studio experience you ever had? Did they ever have to do a retake because of you?

Oh, well you have to acknowledge the fact that there are times when you just need a little more time to work something out. Sometimes it just gets purely scary. Warner Brothers for example, Warner Brothers soundstage. It’s a huge soundstage, like the size of a football field. And in one corner there’s an isolation booth. In another corner there’s an isolation booth. And if you’re in an isolation booth you cannot (which is typically where the guitar gets put) you can’t hear the conductor. And if you don’t have headphones on,

you’re screwed. So it’s like come back from a ten, sit down, they’ve already called the cue. Headphones are on, the clicks, eight free clicks, the baton is up, and you have no idea what we’re playing. And it’s like okay, stop tape. Nowadays it’s much easier. In the old days they had to rack up film. In the old days when I started doing sessions at Paramount in the early 80s, they were running film. They would project film. It was very old school. It was the tail end of the old studio orchestra system. So I’ve had my embarrassing moments. But then sometimes you just nail it. And I’ve had experiences where you just — eight pages of altered tuning 12-string on a Western style score where it’s just acoustic guitar and a string orchestra.
Boy the person who arranged that must have known what the guitar was capable of.
